consensus_summary: The blind consensus identifies 'the Way' primarily as Jesus Christ himself — the exclusive person-path of access to God the Father (John 14:6; Heb 10:19-20) — usually paired with Acts' use of 'the Way' as the earliest name for the Christian movement. Ethical 'two ways' conduct, covenant obedience/Torah walking, and the Isaianic prepared-highway motif are listed as common or minority secondary senses subordinate to the christological identification.
book_summary: The book identifies 'the way' as covenant conduct — the walk of obedient life along God's old paths (Jer 6:16; Matt 7:14) — and explicitly flags 'Jesus Himself as the one way to the Father; the narrow way against the broad' as merely the commonly taught view, signaling departure from it.
consensus_core_identification: The Way = the person of Jesus Christ as the sole means of access to God, with discipleship and the early Christian movement as extensions of that personal identification.
book_core_identification: The way = covenant conduct, i.e., the manner of walking in obedience to God's covenant (the 'old paths' of Jeremiah 6:16), rather than a person.
boundary_disagreement: The book retains texts the consensus also uses (Matt 7:13-14; OT walk/path language) but relocates them from a secondary ethical strand to the controlling definition, while the consensus's controlling texts (John 14:6 person-of-Christ; Acts movement-name) are displaced from the core. Jeremiah 6:16, absent from all four consensus responses, is made a defining proof-text.
material_contradiction: The consensus says the way is fundamentally a person (Christ), of whom conduct is a derivative extension; the book says the way is fundamentally covenant conduct — a mode of behavior — and treats the christological identification as merely 'commonly taught.' A person and a pattern of conduct are different referents; accepting the book's core requires demoting/rejecting the consensus's central personal identification.
rationale: This is not mere boundary adjustment: the book's common-view note explicitly marks the christological reading (John 14:6, narrow-vs-broad) as the popular view distinct from its own definition, and its definition replaces the personal referent with an ethical-covenantal one. That ethical/covenant-walk sense does appear in the consensus lists, but only as a common secondary alternative subordinate to the christological core; elevating it to the exclusive core while displacing Christ-as-way replaces the consensus's central identification rather than refining its edges. Hence DIVERGENT with core CONTRADICTS and PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION on extension (shared texts like Matt 7:14 are kept but re-read; John 14:6/Acts usage is effectively reclassified out of the core).
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the consensus itself concedes 'by extension it denotes the whole life of discipleship,' and covenant obedience is listed as a common alternative, so the book may be seen as narrowing emphasis within an already-acknowledged semantic field rather than contradicting it. If the full chapter harmonizes covenant conduct with Christ embodying that conduct, the readings could be compatible rather than mutually exclusive.
